en: The *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* (Collection from the Jingde Era) by the Chan Master Yongjia, compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuangjue of Shenshui during the Tang Dynasty, is divided into ten chapters.
Chapter One: "The Ritual for Those Who Aspire to the Way. Now, those who wish to cultivate the Way...
First, one must establish one's resolve;
furthermore, the protocols for serving a teacher shall be made manifest as a model of instruction.
Therefore, the first is titled "The Ritual for Aspiring to the Way.
The second is "Restraint of Pride and Extravagance."
Although at first one resolves to cultivate the Way and properly understands the ritual protocols,
if the three karmas become arrogant and extravagant, [the practice will falter].
When the deluded mind is agitated,
how can one attain meditative concentration?
Therefore, the second section clarifies the intention behind the precept against arrogance and luxury.
Third, the purification of the three karmas.
The preceding section on precepts and pride has briefly set forth the essential framework.
Now, by scrutinizing and examining oneself in detail,
one ensures that gross transgressions do not arise;
therefore, it is next explained in sequence how to purely cultivate the three types of action.
The precepts pertain to body, speech, and mind.
This is the fourth verse on *śamatha*.
Having previously examined and reproved body and speech, [one now examines the mind].
One must cause coarse transgressions not to arise;
next, one must enter the gate and follow the gradual stages of cultivating the path.
Not departing from meditative concentration and wisdom;
five ways of giving rise to the mind;
six kinds of analytical discernment.
Therefore, the following four verses clarify *śamatha*;
the fifth verse clarifies *vipaśyanā*.
Without precepts there is no meditation;
without meditation there is no wisdom.
Having already cultivated meditative concentration, [he proceeds].
Because concentration is long-lasting and wisdom is luminous,
the following five verses clarify vipaśyanā;
the sixth verse concerns upeksā.
If one practices concentration exclusively,
after a long time it will lead to sinking;
if one studies wisdom exclusively, [it will lead to agitation].
Because wisdom is predominant and the mind is still in motion,
the sixth section next clarifies the verses on *upavicāra* (mental exploration),
which are equal in measure to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Causing it not to sink or waver,
making concentration and wisdom equal,
and abandoning the two extremes.
Seventh, regarding the gradual progression of the three vehicles:
once concentration and wisdom are balanced,
one is tranquil yet constantly illuminating.
When one contemplates the three [truths] within the single mind,
what doubt remains undispelled?
What illumination remains incomplete?
Although one's own understanding may be clear,
one feels compassion for others who have not yet awakened; furthermore,
there are varying degrees of depth in their awakening.
Therefore, the seventh section next elucidates the gradual progression of the three vehicles.
The eighth section concerns the non-duality of principle and phenomena;
therein, the three vehicles awaken to the principle.
There is no principle that is not thoroughly investigated.
The investigation of principle resides in phenomena;
when phenomena are understood, they are themselves principle.
Therefore, the eighth section next clarifies the non-duality of phenomena and principle—
that phenomena are themselves the truth—
in order to dispel inverted views.
Exhortation to a Friend, Number Nine.
Once phenomena and principle have been harmonized,
the inner mind naturally becomes clear and bright.
Furthermore, I lament that those who study afar waste their precious moments; thus,
I have composed the following nine letters of exhortation to my friends.
The Tenth Vow Text:
Exhorting Friends. Although this involves compassion for others, one must focus the mind single-mindedly on this one goal.
Since one's compassion is not yet universal,
the following text on the sequential cultivation of the aspiration is explained to clarify the vow to deliver all beings.
1. Aspiration for the Way and the Ritual of Conduct, Part One: First, one contemplates the three realms in order to give rise to weary detachment;
next, one draws near to virtuous friends.
This is for the purpose of seeking an exit.
Furthermore, one inquires after their well-being in the morning and evening in order to maintain the proper observance of etiquette.
Next, one examines how [the patient] is responding to treatment,
because it clarifies the state of their nursing and care.
Next, one asks what they are doing.
In order to clarify that one has personally received the teaching,
one next gazes with tireless devotion,
thereby generating a sense of profound reverence.
The frequency and determination are essential for the sake of correct cultivation. Next,
the presentation of the analysis follows according to the understanding.
In order to distinguish between the false and the correct,
one next examines the strength [of the digestion] to know whether it is raw or ripe.
Next, seeing that illness has arisen, one conceives doubt;
because it is capable of being cured by excellent medicine,
one reflects with thorough and precise scrutiny.
In order to seek what is true and correct,
one applies oneself with diligence day and night,
fearing that conditions might diverge.
He focused his mind on a single practice.
For the sake of accomplishing his task,
he sacrificed his life for the Dharma.
For the sake of recognizing their kindness,
if their power of faith is slight and their minds lack single-minded resolve, [they will not attain it].
Their conduct is coarse and their understanding superficial;
they drift along according to circumstances.
When encountering matters, they give rise to thoughts based on those specific events.
If conditions are absent, then the basis for the cessation of mindfulness is also absent.
Since this is neither a contemplation of movement nor stillness,
it accords with the gains and losses of existence and non-existence.
However, the Way is not ascended in vain;
one enters its ranks according to one's merit.
2. Chapter Two: Restraint of Arrogance Regarding Clothing and Food. Regarding the origins of clothing and food: [text continues]
Nurturing and planting;
tilling the soil and digging the earth;
boiling salt and raising silkworm moths.
To bring about maturation through giving is to injure living beings and cause others to undergo death.
Providing for one's own body,
one fears only hunger and cold,
yet does not contemplate the suffering of death.
To kill others to save oneself—
how painful and lamentable! Furthermore,
it employs the fruits of agricultural labor.
The accumulated power [of merit] is profound and vast;
why should it be that sentient beings alone must sacrifice their lives?
It is likewise that the offerings of faith are difficult to exhaust.
"Even though he has left the household life,
what merit does he possess? Alas!"
Now, one who wishes to transcend the three realms has yet to practice the conduct that severs worldly dust;
they merely possess the body of a man in vain.
Yet they lack the resolve of a man;
they merely remain in turmoil from morning until evening and in a state of darkness throughout the night.
Virtue remains uncultivated while food and clothing are squandered; thus,
one deviates from the lofty path of propagating the Way.
Below, I fail to benefit living beings;
in the middle, I am indebted to the four debts of gratitude.
I truly consider this a source of shame.
Therefore, the wise contemplate this:
it is better for a dharma to die than for a non-dharma to arise.
One merely deludes oneself, valuing the body while disparaging the Dharma. 3.
Purifying the Three Karmas through Pure Cultivation. Third: The mental karma of greed, hatred, and false views.
False speech, frivolous talk, double-tongued speech, and harsh words constitute the karmic actions of the mouth;
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the karmic actions of the body.
Now, one who aspires to seek the Great Way—
One must first purify and cultivate the three karmas;
thereafter, within the four modes of deportment,
one gradually enters the Way.
Even unto the objects confronted by the six sense faculties,
one realizes them according to conditions;
thus, both object and cognition are simultaneously quiescent.
Profound indeed is the subtle meaning!
How does one purify the physical karma?
One should reflect deeply within oneself.
In the four modes of conduct— walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—
one restrains and gathers in the three faults.
Do not allow anything to be lost or wasted.
Cherish and nurture all beings with compassion;
do not harm the lives of living creatures.
Whether moving by water, land, or air,
all sentient beings— regardless of the size of their life-span— [are subject to death].
With an impartial mind,
cherish and protect all wriggling and flying creatures,
ensuring that none are harmed or destroyed.
For those caught in the currents of peril and distress,
he diligently rescues them and employs skillful means to deliver them.
They cause all beings to attain liberation;
regarding the wealth and property of others,
they do not take what has not been given.
This extends even to spirits and ghosts;
regarding any object that has an owner,
whether it be a single needle or a blade of grass.
Never intentionally committing offenses,
though living in poverty and begging for alms,
one gives according to what one possesses.
Giving with a respectful mind,
one brings peace and security to others without seeking any reward for their kindness.
He reflected thus:
"The Buddhas of the past practiced *dāna* throughout immeasurable eons."
He gave away elephants, horses, and the seven treasures;
his head, eyes, marrow, and brain;
and even his own body and life.
I renounce it without stinginess;
I am now likewise,
giving whatever is offered to me.
He joyfully made offerings,
his heart free from stinginess,
regarding all forms of female beauty.
The mind is free from defilement and attachment;
yet ordinary beings are inverted,
intoxicated by desire.
Addicted and deluded,
they do not recognize their own transgressions,
like one grasping the stem of a flower.
Failing to realize it is a venomous snake,
the wise person observes its mouth.
The paws of bears and leopards,
or fierce fires and glowing iron—
none of these can serve as a metaphor for it.
Upon copper pillars and iron beds,
their backs are scorched and their entrails are seared;
their flesh and blood are crushed and disintegrated.
With such piercing pain reaching the very marrow of one's heart,
one should contemplate in this way:
there is only suffering, no pleasure.
A leather bag filled with excrement,
a conglomeration of pus and blood,
externally masked by the application of perfumes.
Within, it is nothing but foul and filthy;
impurities flow and overflow,
and it is the dwelling place of maggots and worms.
Even the stench of a fish market or a latrine cannot compare to it.
When the wise contemplate this, they see it clearly.
One sees only hair, body hair, nails, teeth,
thin skin, thick skin,
flesh, blood, sweat, and tears.
Tears, saliva, pus, and fat;
tendons, veins, brain, and meninges;
yellow phlegm and white phlegm.
The liver, gallbladder, marrow, bones, lungs, spleen, kidneys, and stomach;
the heart-fat, bladder,
large intestine, and small intestine.
The raw digestive tract and the cooked digestive tract,
the foul-smelling places of excrement and urine—
such things as these.
Each and every non-human spirit,
stirred and struck by the winds of consciousness,
gives rise to false speech.
They feign friendship while in reality they are resentful and envious;
they ruin one's virtue and obstruct the Path.
This is an exceedingly grave transgression;
one should distance oneself from it as one would avoid an enemy or a bandit.
Therefore, the wise observe them as being like venomous snakes;
they would rather approach a venomous snake than [the former].
Do not consort with women. Why is this?
Because poisonous snakes kill people.
Death and rebirth follow one after another;
bound by female form for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Various forms of torment and suffering are inexhaustible;
examine this with careful attention and deep reflection.
It is difficult to approach;
therefore, the wise thoroughly examine the three vehicles.
Reforming the past and cultivating the future,
turning one's back on evil and following the good,
one refrains from killing and refrains from stealing.
They practice the giving of releasing living beings;
they do not engage in sexual misconduct or impurity;
they constantly cultivate the pure conduct of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Day and night, they were diligent and persevering;
they practiced the Way, performed prostrations,
and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
Aiming for liberation,
one cultivates the three enduring dharmas regarding body, life, and wealth.
One knows that the body is illusory and lacks intrinsic nature;
form is itself emptiness.
Who is this "I"? All phenomena exist merely as provisional designations.
There is no fixed, real entity that constitutes this body;
it is merely the four great elements and the five aggregates.
Each individual part is not the self,
and their combination is likewise non-existent;
thus one seeks [the self] both internally and externally.
Like a mass of foam on water,
a floating bubble, a mirage,
or the illusory transformation of a plantain tree.
Like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water,
they ultimately have no person;
yet, through ignorance, this is not understood.
They falsely grasp at it as a self,
giving rise to perverse craving and attachment toward that which is not real.
Killing, stealing, debauchery,
and wild confusion continue throughout the night and the day.
Though the industrious creation of karma is not ultimately real,
the retribution for good and evil nonetheless follows.
Like a shadow following a form;
when practicing this contemplation,
one does not harbor evil desires.
While sustaining one's body and life,
one should contemplate one's own body as being like a venomous snake.
For the sake of treating illness,
he accepts the four requisites and wears clothing upon his body.
It is like wrapping an ulcer while eating flavorful food with the mouth;
it is like a sick person taking medicine.
Restrain the body and be frugal with speech;
do not give rise to luxury or indulgence.
Upon hearing the teaching on few desires, [one should practice accordingly].
Because they deeply delight in the practice of cultivation, a sutra says:
"One who has few desires and practices dhūta."
One who well knows contentment and sufficiency is able to enter the path of the noble ones. Why is this?
Sentient beings in the evil realms have,
for immeasurable kalpas,
lacked clothing and been destitute of food.
They wail and cry out in agony;
tormented by hunger and cold,
their skin and bones are joined together.
That I am currently temporarily separated from them is not yet sufficient to be considered suffering;
therefore, the wise person—
Valuing the Dharma and disparaging the body,
they diligently seek the ultimate Way,
disregarding even their physical form and life.
This is called the purification of bodily action.
What is the purification of verbal action?
It is to reflect deeply upon the four faults of speech.
It is the root of birth and death,
the augmenter of all evils,
and that which overturns the myriad practices.
They pass criticisms back and forth; therefore,
the wise wish to uproot this source.
One eliminates falsehood and cultivates the four kinds of truthful speech:
upright, gentle, harmonious, and in accordance with reality.
These four phrases are the practice of the wise. Why is this so?
One who speaks with straightforwardness is able to eliminate frivolous speech;
one who speaks with gentleness [is likewise able to do so].
One who is able to eliminate harsh speech is one whose speech is harmonious;
such a person is able to eliminate divisive speech.
One who speaks according to reality is able to eliminate false speech.
There are two types of one who speaks with integrity.
First, he speaks according to the Dharma,
causing all who hear it to understand with clear faith and realization.
Second is the discourse that accords with reason,
which causes all who hear it to eliminate doubt and dispel delusion.
Gentle speech is also of two kinds.
The first is consoling speech,
which causes all who hear it to—
First, they approach with joy;
second, their vocal melodies are pure and elegant,
causing all who hear them to...
One practices with delight and affection.
Regarding those who speak harmonious words, there are also two types.
First, those who harmonize in matters.
Seeing those who are quarreling,
he exhorts and advises them to desist;
he does not praise himself.
To be humble and respectful toward all things;
as for the second, the harmony of principles:
it is to see those who have regressed from the bodhicitta.
He earnestly exhorted him to advance,
skillfully distinguishing between bodhi and afflictions.
They are equal and of one characteristic.
Furthermore, those who speak according to reality are also of two kinds.
First, those whose words accord with the facts.
If it exists, one says it exists;
if it does not exist, one says it does not exist;
if it is so, one says it is so.
If it is not so, one says it is not so.
Second, as for those whose principles are real:
all sentient beings.
All possess Buddha-nature;
the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is eternally abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, the wise practice the four kinds of truthful speech and observe those leaders of the assembly.
Since the beginningless kalpas,
they have been inverted by those four faults and have sunk into the cycle of birth and death.
It is difficult to escape from;
I now wish to uproot its source.
I shall observe that karmic action of speech.
The lips, tongue, teeth,
throat, navel, and vocal resonance are struck and stirred by the wind of consciousness.
Sound issues forth from within this;
due to the causal conditions of the mind,
it is distinguished as being either empty or real.
Truth brings benefit;
falsehood causes diminution.
Truth is the root from which goodness arises.
Emptiness is the root from which evil arises;
it is the fundamental basis of both good and evil,
as manifested through the explanations of spoken words.
The words that describe what is wholesome are called the four right efforts;
the phrases that describe what is unwholesome—
These are called the four perversions.
Perversion leads to suffering;
correctness leads to happiness.
Goodness is the condition that aids the Path;
evil is the root that destroys it.
Therefore, the wise must resolve to support what is correct within their hearts.
Establish yourself in truthful speech;
recite the sutras and mindfully recollect the Buddha;
contemplate the true nature of speech.
When speech leaves nothing behind and both silence and speech are equal,
this is called the pure cultivation of verbal karma.
How does one purify the mental karma?
One reflects deeply upon the source of good and evil.
All arise from the mind;
through the conditions of false thoughts,
one can produce ten thousand evils.
Correctly contemplating causes and conditions can give rise to all manner of goodness;
thus, a sutra says:
The three realms have no separate dharmas;
they are created solely by this one mind.
One should know that the mind is the root of all phenomena.
What is wrong mindfulness?
It is the failure to understand through ignorance,
resulting in the false attachment to a self.
My views are firm;
through greed, hatred, and false views,
I recklessly imagine all that exists.
This gives rise to various attachments and clingings;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Because there is a self."
Thereupon, there arises the notion of "mine.
Because of this notion of "mine," the views of annihilationism and eternalism arise.
The sixty-two views,
the continuous succession of views and afflictions,
and the ninety-eight proclivities.
Birth and death within the three realms cycle without ceasing;
one should know that this is due to perverse thoughts.
It is the root of all evils;
therefore, the wise restrain it and do not follow it.
How does one contemplate it correctly?
That and I are without distinction;
form and mind are not two;
awakening and affliction are likewise so.
The fundamental nature is not differentiated;
birth-and-death and nirvana are equally illuminated as one.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Detached from 'I' and 'mine,' one contemplates equality."
Both "self" and "nirvāṇa" are empty;
one should know that all phenomena are likewise so.
They exist only as names;
thus the Sūtra says:
"Even up to Nirvāṇa."
They are likewise merely names.
It is further said:
"The nature of letters is devoid [of inherent existence]."
Names, too, are empty.
Why is this? Because phenomena do not name themselves.
Provisional names are used to express dharmas;
since dharmas are not truly existent dharmas,
names are likewise not truly existent names.
Names do not correspond to phenomena;
phenomena do not correspond to names.
Names and phenomena have no correspondence.
All things are empty and quiescent.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Dharmas have no names."
Because language is severed,
the wondrous marks transcend names;
true names are not characters.
Why is this? Because it is unconditioned, quiescent,
and supremely subtle.
Severing signs and departing from names,
where the paths of mind and speech are cut off—
know this to be the essential method for right contemplation that returns to the source.
Therefore, the wise person correctly contemplates causes and conditions;
thus all stirrings are dispelled,
and both object and cognition are forgotten together.
When the source of the mind is pure,
this is called the pure cultivation of mental action.
This should be applied to the four modes of deportment.
Regarding that which is confronted by the six sense organs,
one attains clear understanding in accordance with conditions;
such is the sequence for entering the Way.
4. Verses on Śamatha (Verse Four) Precisely when the mind is applied, precisely there is no application of mind.
Without mind, precisely there is application.
In constant practice, there is simply nothingness. Now,
mindfulness does not mean forgetting sensory objects,
yet it does not cease to engage with them.
It is not that one ceases mindfulness while failing to forget objects;
rather, when one forgets, then mindfulness ceases and objects are forgotten.
When mindfulness ceases, then objects are forgotten and [the mind] comes to rest.
Forgetting the dust of the senses, one rests;
in this resting, there is nothing that can rest.
By resting the thoughts, one forgets.
Forgetting, there is nothing to be forgotten;
forgetting, there is nothing to be forgotten.
It is free from the dust of worldly traces and beyond all opposition.
The breath has nothing that can cause it to cease;
the cessation of thought is not through knowledge.
Knowledge of cessation is the counterpart to relinquishment.
It is perpetually dark and tranquil;
utterly still and without dependence.
Its wondrous nature is innate.
Just as fire is extinguished of its own accord when it encounters emptiness,
emptiness is a metaphor for the wondrous nature that is devoid of marks.
Fire is compared to the non-arising of deluded thoughts.
The passage says:
"After forgetting conditions, there is profound stillness."
The nature of numinous awareness is vividly distinct;
that which is indeterminate and obscure is brilliantly clear;
the realization of the true, original emptiness is perfectly manifest.
Vigilant stillness is correct;
insentient stillness is not.
Stillness that is vigilant is correct.
If distracted thoughts are alert, they are not [true] non-thought;
if one uses cognition to cognize stillness,
this is not cognition without an object.
It is like a hand grasping a wish-fulfilling gem;
it is not that there is no wish-fulfilling gem in the hand.
If one knows by means of self-cognition, [it is so].
Nor is it a cognition without an object,
just as a hand that has formed a fist is not a hand that is not a fist.
Nor does it know the knowledge of stillness,
nor does it know itself as knowing;
yet it cannot be said to be without knowledge.
Because its intrinsic nature is luminously clear,
it is not the same as wood or stone;
yet the hand does not grasp the wish-fulfilling gem.
Nor does one form a fist oneself;
yet it cannot be said that there are no hands,
for the hands remain at ease.
It is not like a rabbit's horn.
Furthermore, regarding the gradual stages of cultivating the mind:
one knows objects by means of cognition.
When an object exists, cognition also exists.
If one uses cognition to cognize cognition,
then that cognition which cognizes is separated from the object.
When an object has departed, one still knows it exists;
when cognition arises, one knows that knowing.
If subsequent cognition were to arise at that time, [the same would apply].
The prior cognition has already ceased long ago;
since two cognitions cannot coexist,
only the cessation of the prior cognition is possible.
The locus of cessation is the object of knowledge;
both subject and object are unreal.
In the former case, cessation brings about the cessation of cognition.
Subsequently, one knows that cognition follows upon cessation;
as birth and cessation continue in succession,
this is the path of saṃsāra.
What is now called "knowing" does not require knowing that one knows;
it is simply knowing.
Thus, the preceding does not connect with the ceasing,
and the succeeding does not give rise [to it];
the preceding and succeeding are severed and discontinuous.
In the interim, it remains solitary;
in its very essence, it disregards all else;
and it is extinguished as soon as it arises.
Once the essence of cognition has already ceased,
one suddenly feels as if resting in emptiness;
for a brief moment, all is tranquil and still.
Awakening alone is non-apprehension; that is,
awakening is the absence of awakening—
the awakening of non-awakening.
It is different from wood or stone;
this is the state of the initial mind,
where all thoughts are extinguished in profound stillness.
Suddenly identical to one who is dead,
subject and object are instantly forgotten,
and all subtle conditions are utterly purified.
Utterly still and voidly quiescent,
it seems as if devoid of cognition;
yet this nature of non-cognition—
It is different from wood or stone;
this is the state of the initial mind,
which is difficult to comprehend.
When entering the initial stage of the mind,
three things should not exist:
first, evil.
The first refers to reflecting on the causes and conditions of the five worldly sensual desires.
The second refers to the wholesome,
which means reflecting on various mundane virtuous matters.
The three types of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) refer to states where one does not contemplate good or evil, remaining in a state of silent, dull stagnation.
Within the context of the precepts, these three must be fully possessed.
First, the precept of restraining from misconduct,
which means abandoning all evil;
second, the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas.
The first refers to the cultivation of all virtues;
the third is the precept of benefiting sentient beings,
which means vowing to deliver all living beings.
Within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), three aspects must be distinguished.
First is abiding in concentration (*sthiti-samādhi*):
this refers to the wondrous nature that is natural and fundamentally unmoving from the beginning.
Second is the concentration that induces meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
which refers to the mind becoming clarified, tranquil, lucid, and increasingly radiant.
Third is the concentration that accomplishes tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-samādhi*).
This means that when the water of meditative concentration (samādhi) solidifies into clarity, all phenomena are reflected therein.
Within wisdom, three types must be distinguished.
The first is the wisdom of emptiness (śūnyatā-prajñā).
This means realizing that the aggregates (skandhas) are not the self;
that within the aggregates there is no self,
just like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
Second is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-prajñā*). This refers to the realization that all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*),
are dependently designated and lack substantial reality.
Like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water,
it is the wisdom of the threefold emptiness;
that is to say, the knowledge that realizes both the object and the cognition are empty.
This emptiness is also empty.
Among these three, one must recognize:
first, the view of emptiness.
The first is the view of emptiness while seeing what is not empty;
the second is the view of non-emptiness,
which means seeing what is not empty while seeing it as something other than non-empty.
The third is the view of the emptiness of the three natures (*trisvabhāva-śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*).
This refers to seeing intrinsic nature while simultaneously seeing the absence of nature;
one must distinguish between these three [aspects] within the biased [view].
First, there is the Dharma-body without prajñā and liberation;
second, there is prajñā without the liberation of the Dharma-body;
third, there is liberation without the Dharma-body and prajñā.
Because it is one and not two, it is not complete;
because it is not complete, it is not the true nature.
Furthermore, the three [aspects] within the partial must be distinguished.
First, there is the dharma-body and prajñā, but no liberation;
second, there is prajñā and liberation, but no dharma-body;
third, there is liberation and the dharma-body, but no prajñā.
Because two exist and one is absent, it is not complete;
because it is not complete, it is not the true nature.
Within completeness, all three must be present.
The single Dharma-body being free from delusion is Prajñā;
Prajñā being without attachment is Liberation;
Liberation being quiescent extinction is the Dharma-body.
Second, non-attachment to prajñā is itself liberation;
liberation and quiescence are themselves the dharmakāya;
and the dharmakāya’s freedom from delusion is itself prajñā.
The tranquility of the three liberations is the Dharma-body;
the non-delusion of the Dharma-body is Prajñā;
the non-attachment of Prajñā is liberation.
To raise one is to possess all three;
it is said that the three bodies are identical to the one.
These are the three virtues within the causal state.
These are not the three virtues on the level of the fruit.
If one wishes to know the three virtues on the level of the fruit:
the Dharma-body possesses the virtue of severance.
Because virtues are manifested through the abandonment of afflictions,
it is called the "virtue of abandonment.
The self-enjoyment body possesses the virtue of wisdom.
Because they possess the true merits of the four wisdoms,
the two bodies of the other-transformed [nirmāṇakāya] and the enjoyment [saṃbhogakāya] possess great beneficent virtue.
